claims.text: The business cycle is the repeated rise and fall in the total output of an economy over time, traditionally described in four stages: growth, boom, recession and slump.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The stages run in sequence: in growth output recovers and rises, in boom output peaks at its highest level, in recession output falls, and in slump output bottoms out at its lowest point.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The cycle repeats rather than settling: a slump is followed by renewed growth as demand builds again, so the economy passes through the stages again and again.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level over time, which means each unit of money buys less than it did before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When employment rises, more households earn wages, so consumer spending tends to rise and the demand reaching businesses usually lifts with it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When inflation rises, a business's bought-in materials and wage bills usually rise with it, which squeezes the margin between cost and price unless the increase can be passed on to customers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the total value of the goods and services an economy produces in a year; rising GDP usually signals rising incomes and stronger demand, and falling GDP usually signals weaker demand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A recession and inflation are different conditions: a recession is total output falling over time, while inflation is the general price level rising, so an economy can experience either one without the other.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The economic objectives a government typically pursues are rising Gross Domestic Product (GDP), low unemployment and low, stable inflation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Governments pursue these objectives because rising GDP tends to create jobs and tax revenue, while low inflation and low unemployment help households plan and spend with confidence.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Government spending is the money a government pays out on the goods, services and projects it provides, from roads and schools to public works.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rise in an indirect tax, such as fuel duty, is collected as part of the price of the taxed item, which tends to reduce the quantity demanded and can leave affected businesses with lower sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rise in income tax lowers the disposable income households have left after tax, so spending on many consumer goods tends to fall, which usually reduces the revenue of businesses that sell them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rise in government spending, on roads, schools or public works for example, tends to raise the demand reaching the businesses that supply those projects and the workers the projects pay.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money, charged as a percentage of the loan for each period of the loan, and at the same time the reward a saver receives for keeping money deposited.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: When interest rates rise, borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more attractive, so businesses tend to postpone loans and investment, and demand for expensive goods bought on credit, such as vehicles, often falls.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Interest rates and taxes are different instruments: an interest rate is the price of borrowing charged by whoever lends the money, while a tax is a charge on income, spending or profits owed to the state.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses commonly respond to economic changes by adjusting prices, output levels, staffing plans, borrowing and marketing, choosing the response that fits the change they face.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The best response depends on the business's objective and situation: a business aiming for profit may respond to falling demand by cutting its costs, while one aiming to grow its market share may instead hold prices and accept a lower margin for a time.
